en: In the sacrifice, Satyavatī obtained from the great seer Parāśara a son who possessed vast knowledge and supreme prosperity, even as she was in the midst of the island.
To him, who dispels the darkness of ignorance from the mind. ||1||
Just as the ocean is exceedingly vast and as the Himavat mountain is likewise,
both renowned as treasuries of jewels, so too is the Bhārata described.
This narrative is constantly relied upon by the best of poets, just as a noble lord is depended upon by servants seeking advancement. (3)
From this supreme history, the insights of poets are born, just as the three arrangements of the world arise from the five elements. (4)
Without relying on this narrative, how could the world exist? It would be like the maintenance of a body without depending on food. (5)
But having heard this narrative, no other thing is pleasing to hear,
just as the cry of a raven is not pleasing after hearing the song of the male cuckoo.
The purpose of life, O bull among the Bharatas, lies in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
whatever is found here may be found elsewhere, but what is not here is nowhere else.
Among all beings, a human indeed exists within both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
one should cause that which is possessed by the inauspicious to abide in the auspicious alone.
One should not let oneself be dejected even when deprived of enjoyments;
for even in the state of a Caṇḍāla, human birth is in every way difficult to obtain.
For this is the primary womb, O Lord of the World, reaching which one is able to save oneself through actions characterized by auspiciousness. (4)
He who does not seek a cure for the disease of hell while still here—having gone to that place where no medicine exists, what will he do, afflicted as he is by pain? (5)
Having attained this human state, which is so difficult to find and serves as a staircase to heaven,
one should so compose oneself that one does not fall away from it again.
O Brahmin, this is considered the land of action, while that is the land of fruition;
whatever action one performs here is experienced there in the next world. (7)

Having attained this human birth, which is difficult to find and as flickering as a flash of lightning, one should direct the mind toward the destruction of worldly existence and toward the cultivation of the means for liberation. (8)
That man who, having obtained a human birth so difficult to attain, becomes a despiser of Dharma and a slave to desire out of greed, is utterly deceived. ||9||
Human birth is extremely difficult to attain and is comparable to a flash of lightning;
having obtained it, if one does not depart from cyclic existence, one is deceived. (10)
With my arms raised high, I cry out, yet no one listens to me.
From dharma come both wealth and pleasure; why, then, is it not practiced? (11)
One who desires wealth and pleasure should practice dharma from the very beginning;
for neither wealth nor pleasure ever departs from dharma.
They honor the righteous, not the wealthy nor the lustful;
for there is no fraction of happiness in wealth, whereas in dharma there is supreme happiness. (13)
For those who desire heaven, Dharma alone is the raft and nothing else;
it is like one's own boat for a person wishing to reach the further shore of the ocean. (14)
For effort made for the sake of desire, wealth, or liberation may indeed fail;
however, an undertaking for the sake of Dharma—even a mere intention—is never fruitless. (15)
Just as the rising sun indeed dispels all darkness, so too one who abides in what is auspicious dispels all evil. (16)
For in whatever way a person’s mind delights in what is wholesome, in that very way all his goals are accomplished; there is no doubt about this. ||17||
Dharma is always beneficial to men, and Dharma alone is the refuge of the virtuous;
from Dharma, O dear one, the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile, have come forth. (18)
He whose intellect, following the path of Dharma, does not deviate—him they call a performer of meritorious deeds, beyond the grief of friends and kinsmen. (19)
Just as water sprinkled here for the sake of sugarcane also thoroughly moistens the grasses and even the creepers, so too does a person wandering about, drenched by the rain of Dharma.
He attains words, desires, and riches. ||20||
For every person obtains beauty, personal virtues, extensive lineage, and the accumulation of abundant wealth, exactly as they have been performed [in previous lives].
Always [prosper] by means of the virtuous action performed by oneself. ||21||
In wildernesses, forest fortresses, and difficult calamities, in times of agitation,
and when weapons are raised, those who possess righteousness have no fear.
For those of auspicious deeds, there are beautiful women who are well-adorned and pleasing to the mind, and they dwell upon the rooftops of palatial residences. (23)
Just as frogs come to a water-trough and birds to a full lake, so do companions and riches come to those of virtuous deeds. (24)
A wise man, established like an immortal, should acquire both knowledge and wealth;
yet, as if seized by the hair by Death himself, he should practice dharma.
If people could see death residing upon their own heads,
even food would no longer be palatable, let alone the performance of worldly duties.
One should seek righteousness while young; one should seek wealth while young; one should seek sacred learning while young.
Indeed, when one falls into the state of a beast, one neither rises up nor finds knowledge. (27)
It is my opinion that he who is peaceful in the early stage of life is truly peaceful;
for when the bodily constituents are wasting away, who does not possess tranquility? (28)
A child is so in relation to youth, and a youth is so in relation to old age;
having ascended the lap of death, what stability can one expect? (29)
Before the Ender (Death), with Disease as his charioteer, forcibly shatters the body at the exhaustion of life, one should zealously gather great merit. (30)
One should be virtuous in conduct like a youth, for life is indeed impermanent;
who indeed knows when death’s army will fall upon one this very day? (31)
Relatives, together with their kinsmen, turn back at the edge of the funeral pyre;
therefore, perform that meritorious deed by which you may go together with them. (32)
Having abandoned the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, people remain near it for a moment out of attachment and then turn their faces away and depart. (33)
One quality is the highest good: patience alone is called peace;
one thing is the supreme contentment: non-violence alone brings happiness. (34)
If there were only one treatise, the highest good would undoubtedly be attained;
however, because of the multiplicity of treatises here, the highest good has been concealed. (35)
"Do not, my dear son, treat the elderly with contempt; learn from them and acquire their wisdom.
For the course of Dharma is subtle and difficult to follow, like that of a serpent. (36)
Dharma is declared to be the Śruti, which is the Veda; the Dharmaśāstra, however, is Smṛti.
One should investigate all matters by means of these two; from them, Dharma is extracted.
The four castes, as well as the worlds and the four stages of life separately—the past, the present, and the future—all are established from the Veda. (38)
One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas;
for the Veda fears one of little learning, thinking, "He will misrepresent me. (39)
The supreme dharma is that declared in the Śrutis, as is the other found in the Smṛtis; the conduct of the learned (śiṣṭācāra) is proclaimed as the highest—these are the three eternal dharmas. ||40||
"O dear one, one should not practice toward another that which is contrary to oneself; this is the Dharma in brief. Anything other than this proceeds from desire. (41)
But those who are disciplined, well-restrained, devoted to truth and uprightness, and have ascended the path of dharma—follow their conduct. (42)
Of dharma, which revolves in every direction like the wheel of a chariot,
no fixed certainty can be found, just as none can be found for the father of a son born of a courtesan.
Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be held fast:
do not toward others practice those things which are disagreeable to yourself. (44)
Like husks among grains of rice, or like gnats among birds, such are those among men for whom dharma is not the motive. (45)
Ordinary people die for the sake of birth and are born for the sake of death; they do not live for the sake of Dharma nor for the sake of spiritual action, like blades of grass. (46)
But those people who, possessed by delusion of intellect, do not respect the Dharma—they suffer even as they follow those traveling on the wrong path. (47)
Those dull-witted people who delight in unrighteousness and are destined for rebirth as animals, having entered into a miserable womb, do not find happiness. (48)
Acquire that wealth which brings no fear from kings or thieves, and which does not abandon you when you have died. (49)
If one’s dharma does not perish, even while living on a mere skull, one should realize, "I am wealthy"; for the virtuous consider dharma alone to be true wealth.
If one who practices the Dharma should find that their livelihood does not come to them, would even the gleanings of grain, water, vegetables, and so forth, surely not fail them? (51)
In the forests there are peaceful vegetables and rivers of pure water;
the moon is a common lamp—what need is there for worldly riches? (52)
For even while occupied with other matters, one's own interest is pursued from time to time;
indeed, even when struck on the back, a cow continues to eat mouthful by mouthful as she wanders about. (53)
By the Buddha, who has attained tranquility and self-control, and who is ever-exerted in spirit, the course of the Dharma must be sought, just as the path of a fish is sought within the waters. (54)
The four castes are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya; these three castes are the twice-born.
The fourth is the once-born Śūdra; there is no fifth here. ||55||
A Brāhmaṇa should indeed study, perform sacrifices, give gifts, and visit the foremost of sacred fords;
he should also teach and officiate at sacrifices for those who are entitled to do so.
Or he may accept gifts that are prescribed by rule. ||56||
Dharma, truth, austerity, self-control, freedom from envy, modesty, endurance, lack of malice,
sacrifice, charity, fortitude, and forgiveness.
Indeed, there are twelve great vows for a Brāhmaṇa. ||57||
Having studied the Vedas, having fully tended the sacred fires, having sacrificed with rituals, having protected the subjects,
and having supported his dependents, kinsmen, and relatives;
Having given a gift, a kṣatriya goes to heaven. ||58||
Having studied, the Vaiśya should at the proper time share his wealth with Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, as well as with those who have sought his protection;
he should first inhale the holy smoke of the three sacred fires.
Having passed away, he enjoys the pleasures of the gods in heaven. ||59||
The Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya caste, and the Śūdra— honoring these in due order according to the law—
one becomes free from distress and has one's sins burnt away when they are satisfied.
Having abandoned the body, he enjoys the pleasures of heaven. ||60||
A cowardly kshatriya, a brahmin who eats all things, a vaishya devoid of effort, a low-caste man who is lazy,
and a high-born man who is learned yet ill-behaved and lacking in conduct.
A Brahmin fallen from truth and a woman who is corrupt. ||61||
O King, one who is full of passion, one who is liberated, one who cooks for his own sake, a fool, a talkative person, and a kingdom devoid of a king—
all these, O King, fall into a state of pitiable wretchedness.
And he who is unrighteous and devoid of affection for his subjects. ||62||
"Sincerity, compassion, self-restraint, and control of the senses—Manu has declared this to be the common duty for all four social orders. (63)
Non-violence, truthful speech, and straightforwardness toward all beings, as well as forbearance and vigilance—he who possesses these shall be happy. (64)
Everything crooked is the path of death; straightforwardness is the path of Brahman.
Such is the scope of knowledge; what will mere idle talk accomplish?
Compassion is the supreme dharma; forgiveness is the supreme strength;
self-knowledge is the supreme knowledge; and the vow of truth is the supreme vow.
Just as people avoid thorns, pits, and fire,
so do people avoid a man who performs cruel deeds.

For self-restraint is indeed superior to giving; while giving is a cause for worldly advancement, the self-restrained person does not become angry. Therefore, self-restraint is greater than giving. (68)
For one whose limbs are merely moistened with water is not called "bathed";
he alone is bathed who is bathed in self-restraint, for he is pure both externally and internally. (69)
He who does not rejoice in great gain nor grieve in calamity, and whose wisdom is well-restrained, is proclaimed as one who is self-controlled. (70)
The senses alone constitute all that is both heaven and hell;
when restrained they lead to heaven, and when unleashed they lead to hell. (71)
The restraint of the senses nourishes life, virtuous conduct, security, strength, self-control, as well as dharma and artha. //72//
One should practice the ten paths of action: three by means of the mind, four by means of speech, and likewise three by means of the body. ||73||
One should practice in three ways with the mind: non-covetousness regarding the property of others, benevolence toward all sentient beings, and the conviction that there is a fruit for actions. (74)
O King of kings, one should neither utter nor even contemplate these four verbal faults: idle chatter, harshness, slander, and falsehood. (75)
One should completely avoid these three bodily evils in every respect: the taking of life, theft, and likewise adultery with another's wife. (76)
Whatever one habitually practices through body, mind, or speech—that very thing carries one away; therefore, one should practice what is wholesome. //77//
A person endowed with virtue is rare in speech, action, and thought;
but a person whose conduct is of such a kind as this is rare indeed among all people. (78)
Having made a resolution with the mind through the mind, it is then expressed by speech;
afterwards it is carried out by action; therefore, the mind is indeed the primary factor. (79)
For the mind is the root from which all the sense faculties proceed; it is well-established that their activity in both auspicious and inauspicious states depends upon it. (80)
He whose mind—which wanders far, travels in many directions, and consists of longing and doubt—is well-restrained, is happy both in this world and after death. 81.
One who possesses vision sees everything with the eye joined to the mind;
when the mind has become distracted, one does not see even while seeing. (82)
People are generally deceived by mental distinctions regarding the lack of difference between the private parts of a woman and a moist, oozing wound. (83)
The world recoils at the word "red," yet craves it as "mouth-nectar";
thus people are deceived by these self-coined words that carry the notion of a "self. 84.
Even toward identical objects, the activity of the mind differs;
a son thinks of the breast in one way, and a husband in another. (85)
Regarding the single body of a woman, three different perceptions arise in a wandering mendicant, a lustful man, and a dog: [it is] a corpse, a mistress, and food, respectively. (86)
The purity of intention of a person should be understood as the determining factor in all actions;
otherwise, a beloved wife is kissed with one kind of intent, while a daughter is kissed with another. (87)
One who is covetous and envious of the possessions of others finds no joy either in this world or in the next;
therefore, one who desires constant happiness should abandon covetousness. (88)
A person should always maintain a mind that is concentrated upon all beings;
he should not covet, nor should he long for, nor should he think of anything improper or unreal. 89.
Restrain, restrain, and thoroughly control the senses as well as the mind, regarding those objects of sound and the other [senses] which are forbidden, difficult to obtain, and harmful. (90)
For one who feels envy toward the wealth, beauty, prowess, lineage, happiness, intellect, and good deeds of others, that disease is endless. (91)
This world belongs to the patient, and the next world belongs to the patient;
in this life they receive honor, and in the next, a fortunate rebirth. (92)
O dear one, there is nothing else more glorious or more beneficial than this:
that for a powerful man, forgiveness is always and everywhere the best course. (93)
If there were no people among humans who were as patient as the earth, there would be no friendship among men, for conflict has its root in anger. (94)
He who casts away arisen anger through forbearance alone, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin—he indeed is called a true man. (95)
Enemies do not go to their destruction even for one who slays them throughout his entire life;
however, for one who knows how to restrain anger, no hater exists. (96)
That which is not born of disease, yet is bitter, causes headache,
robs one of fame, and results in the arising of evil fruits— that which the virtuous drink, but the wicked do not drink.
Drink up your wrath, O Great King, and be at peace. ||97||
But that person here who treats all beings as himself, who has laid aside the rod of punishment and conquered anger, thrives in happiness after death. (98)
But a man who has conceived enmity always sleeps in misery, with an unpeaceful mind, like a snake in its dwelling. (99)
Where is sleep for one who is ill, or for one who is terrified or indignant;
or again, for one who is brooding over wealth or longing for sensual pleasure? (100)
One who is free from anger is superior to those who are angry; likewise, one who is patient is superior to one who is impatient.
And humans are superior to non-humans.
In the same way, the wise man is preeminent over the ignorant. ||101||
Whatever one who is angry sacrifices, whatever he gives, whatever austerity he performs, or whatever oblation he offers—
all that Vaivasvata seizes from him.
The exertion of one who is prone to anger becomes futile. ||102||
One should always protect one's ascetic merit from anger, one's prosperity from envy, one's knowledge from honor and dishonor, and one's self from negligence. (103)
Anger is Yama, the son of Vivasvat; death is the river Vaitaraṇī;
knowledge is the wish-fulfilling cow; and contentment is the Nandana grove. (104)
An angry man commits sins; an angry man may even kill his teachers;
an angry man may insult even the virtuous with harsh speech. (105)
An enraged person never discerns what should or should not be said;
for one who is angry, there is nothing that ought not to be done, and nothing that ought not to be spoken at any time. 106.
O best of men, anger is the enemy residing within the bodies of human beings;
he who abandons both anger and greed shall attain honor in this world. (107)
Anger should be especially restrained toward deities, kings, and Brahmins, as well as toward children, the elderly, and the sick. (108)
For the sake of the Dharma and its purpose, the patient endurance of one who practices forbearance is supreme peace;
indeed, that is attained through fortitude for the sake of gathering the world. 109.
One should avoid atheism, atheistic views, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities; one should also avoid hatred, hypocrisy, pride, anger, and harshness. ||110||
Even if the next world is uncertain, the wise should certainly abandon what is unwholesome;
for if it does not exist, what loss is there? But if it does exist, the nihilist is ruined.

The wise do not know the next world through direct perception, as it has never been seen before; however, having transcended the scriptures, that which is to be believed must be understood by the discerning person. 112.
The lack of authority in the Vedas, the transgression of the scriptures, and universal instability—this is the destruction of the self. (113)
Place with confidence to your left that man who is an atheist, who has broken all bounds of propriety, and who stands like a wind at the edge of a river—like dust raised up by a gale. (114)
Those who are nihilists, inactive, transgressors of their gurus and scriptures, violent, and of evil conduct, become short-lived. (115)
Those who increase their flesh and blood strive for things of this world; they are utterly nihilistic, being fast asleep regarding matters pertaining to the next world. (116)
A man who performs two actions in this world is honored:
by not speaking any harsh words, and likewise by not seeking the wealth of the wicked. (117)
One should speak briefly and correctly with an undistracted mind;
for a continuous flow of speech arises either from passion or from dispassion. (118)
Well-spoken speech brings about various kinds of prosperity;
that same speech, when ill-spoken, results in misfortune for men. (119)
Word-arrows fly forth from the mouth;
struck by them, one grieves day and night,
for they fall upon the vital organs.
Therefore, a wise person should not release [anger] toward others. ||120||
Fierce words burn the vital points, the bones, the heart, and the life-breaths of men in this world;
therefore, one should avoid speech that is harsh and cruel in form.
One who delights in the Dharma should avoid her even at the last. ||121||
A forest struck down by an axe grows back slowly;
but that wound caused by a loathsome word spoken is never healed. 122.
One should not despise those who have missing limbs or extra limbs, those devoid of learning, those who are censured, those lacking beauty or wealth, or those who are weak in spirit. (123)
One should not desire to revile, nor speak falsehoods,
nor engage in slander or idle gossip;
being committed to truth, moderate in speech, and vigilant.
It enters into a state of protection, with the door of speech closed.
That man who speaks with praise to one's face but reviles them behind their back is like a dog in this world; he has lost his way toward the higher realms. 125.
One should certainly not utter slander, nor should it ever be heard;
one should either cover one's ears or depart from that place elsewhere. 126.
In this world, even an atheist would tremble before a man who has fallen from truth and righteousness as if before an enraged venomous serpent; how much more so, then, a believer? (127)
Truth and immortality, as well as death—these two are established within the body.
Through delusion one encounters death; through truth one attains immortality. 128.
For neither sacrifices, nor gifts, nor religious observances can deliver a person as truth alone does in this world, O bull among men. (129)
Among men, the Brahmin is supreme; among radiant things, the sun is supreme; among all limbs, the head is supreme; and among all virtues, truth is supreme. (130)
That lowest of men who, for the sake of another, betrays his own word—what would he not do for his own sake, that sinner destined for the hells? (131)
One should speak words that are truthful, non-harming, and not slanderous; they should be timely, gentle, free from cruelty, and devoid of backbiting. (132)
When asked about an object seen or experienced, one who does not conceal it, but speaks exactly as it is—this is the characteristic of truth. (133)
Speech that is factual is not necessarily truth, nor is speech that is not factual necessarily false.
That which is exceedingly beneficial to living beings is truth; the other is falsehood. (134)
Life is the cause for the maintenance of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
by one who destroys it, what is not destroyed? For protection is for the sake of the welfare of all beings.
How could one who desires life for himself wish to kill another?
Whatever one desires for oneself, that one should consider for others as well. (136)
What man would maintain this body by inflicting pain upon others, at the end of which even a dog places its feet fearlessly upon his head? (137)
If the ultimate end of this body is to become worms or ashes, why is it protected by being pampered and oppressed? (138)
Whether walking or standing, waking or even sleeping, his every action is for the sake of the welfare of living beings; it is like the behavior of a beast. (139)
The lioness gives birth to one, while the she-wolf gives birth to many offspring;
those being devoured by the former do not meet their end in any way whatsoever.
He who does not inflict killing, binding, or affliction upon living beings, desiring the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness. (141)
Whatever one thinks of, whatever one finds pleasure in, and wherever one forms an attachment—to that very thing one attains without effort; and he does not harm any living beings. (142)
Those self-disciplined men who desire to obtain beauty, physical integrity, full lifespan, wisdom, dexterity, and mindfulness must avoid violence. (143)
He who, devoted to compassion, grants fearlessness to all beings, to him all beings grant fearlessness in this world; of this there is no doubt. (144)

Whatever loss there may be toward all sentient beings, and whatever compassion there is for even a single sentient being—indeed, compassion alone is superior to the giving away of all sentient beings. (145)
For indeed, nothing in this world is found to be dearer than one's own life; therefore, a person should practice compassion toward others just as toward oneself. 146.
Free from anger, truthful in speech, non-injurious toward living beings, free from envy, and of virtuous conduct, one shall attain a long life. (147)
Born into low families, afflicted by many diseases, of evil conduct, and prone to violence, these sinful beings become short-lived, crying out in pain due to the arising of dejection. (148)

Those men who, relying on their own strength, take away the wealth of others which ought not to be stolen, do not take it for the sake of Dharma; they merely plunder it, of this there is no doubt. (149)
A man who, having seized the property of another, dwells in comfort, is suspicious of everything like a thief, like a wild animal that has entered a village. (150)
Those of the highest vows declare that there are only three treasures for a man:
he should not bear malice, he should be compassionate, and he should always speak the truth. (151)
That mode of conduct which does not cause harm toward suffering kinsmen, friends, or those who have sought refuge is compassion that is exceedingly weighty. (152)
One must never, under any circumstances, go to the wives of others among any of the social classes;
for there is nothing so detrimental to longevity as the pursuit of another's wife. (153)
Therefore, one who is wise, disciplined, and possessed of both theoretical knowledge and realized insight, and who desires long life, should not even in his mind serve the wives of others. 154.
That very same pleasure of touch, and that same mockery at the end, is found with one's own wives as with other women; what, then, is the advantage in the wives of others? (155)
Therefore, O Suśīla, a person should not perform unwholesome deeds through speech, body, or mind;
for whatever wholesome or unwholesome one performs, one experiences the fruit thereof. (156)
Abstaining from malice toward living beings through body, mind, and speech, as well as showing favor and practicing generosity—this the wise know to be ethical discipline (śīla). 157.
O Great King, it is certain that *dha* represents truth, *tha* conduct, *ba* strength, and *ja* indeed the fifth; there is never any doubt in this matter. (158)
For by means of ethical discipline, the three worlds can indeed be conquered; of this there is no doubt.
Indeed, nothing whatsoever in the world is impossible for one who is firmly established in ethical discipline. (159)
Virtue is paramount, O Pūya; for he whose virtue perishes here has no purpose served by victory—what is the use of one who is ill-behaved? (160)
One should never honor even a superior person who is devoid of good character;
however, one should honor even a Śūdra who knows the Dharma and possesses virtuous conduct. ||161||
Dharma is protected by conduct; knowledge is protected by application;
beauty is protected by grooming; and family lineage is protected by character. ||162||
A man of noble birth proclaims himself by means of the auspicious results arising from his own conduct and behavior;
likewise, a man [proclaims himself] even when his own lineage has perished.
Furthermore, he brings forth illumination through his own virtuous conduct. ||163||
All the Vedas together with their six auxiliary limbs, Sāṃkhya, the Purāṇas, and birth in a noble family—
none of these constitute the ultimate goal.
O King, for a man who is devoid of virtuous conduct, ||164||
Neither kinsmen, nor wealth, nor learning, nor sacred scripture, nor secret spells, nor valor—
none of these have the power to protect one from suffering.
But in the other world, it is in ethical discipline, not in that [other] world. ||165||
He who shows favor to the world when it is poor and dejected in spirit attains increase in sons and cattle, as well as imperishable fame. (166)
He who shows favor even to an enemy who has come to him in distress seeking refuge—that man alone is truly called a man. 167.
Generosity is a caravan for one traveling abroad; a wife is a friend for one staying at home;
a physician is a friend for the sick; and generosity is a friend for one who is dying. (168)
Neither mother nor father accomplishes anything for anyone; a living being, whose provisions for the journey are his own generosity, experiences the fruit of his own karma. 169
The wise have declared that non-miserliness consists in generosity, restraint regarding the Dharma, and constant steadfastness; for through renunciation, one attains what is auspicious. (170)
"Through generosity one becomes wealthy; through service to the elders, wise;
and through non-violence, long-lived—so say the sages. (171)
Nothing in the three worlds is found to be more difficult than giving;
for there is great thirst for wealth, and yet it is obtained with hardship. (172)
"Alas, they perform what is difficult indeed, those who renounce great wealth; yet we are unable to renounce even these things that are worthless. (173)
What virtue is there in one who possesses wealth yet does not give it to those in need?
Wealth has but one true course: giving; all others lead to ruin. (174)
The wise should relinquish both wealth and even life for the sake of another;
it is better to abandon them for a worthy cause, for a virtuous woman is led to ruin when they are destroyed.
Give and eat abundantly; do not be miserly people. Hoards are exhausted by the depletion of karma, not by enjoyment. (176)

The Vedas have the Agnihotra sacrifice as their fruit; wealth has the giving and enjoying of it as its fruit; a woman has pleasure and sons as her fruit; and sacred learning has good character and conduct as its fruit. (177)
What is the use of wealth with which one neither gives nor enjoys?
What is the use of strength with which one does not subdue enemies? What is the use of sacred learning with which one does not practice righteousness?
Of what use is a self for one who has not conquered the senses and is not self-controlled?
He whose wealth comes and goes without being fruitful through giving, though he breathes like a blacksmith's bellows, does not truly live. 179.
For in this world, the gift of fearlessness toward living beings surpasses all other gifts;
he who first abandons even his own sharp body [attains it].
He attains infinite fearlessness from all creatures. ||180||
The qualities of the place, the time, the recipient, the field, the object, the donor, and the intention are the causes for the excellence of the fruit of even a well-performed gift. (181)
O tiger among men, these two stand above heaven:
the giver of food during a famine, and the giver of gold during times of plenty. 182.
Whatever is given to others on the occasions of the six Aśītimukhas,
during eclipses of the moon and sun, and to Viṣṇu— that is inexhaustible.

Even those who have undergone the mortification of breath-exercises and attained great powers through their practice will not, if they give wealth acquired by unjust means, benefit others even by the thousands. (184)
One should not give wealth to the unworthy, nor speak words to the wicked, nor eat food from them; one should not take from the virtuous, nor should one seek refuge with the unrighteous. 185.
If there were no Brahmin endowed with learning and virtuous conduct to receive the gift, the wealth of the wealthy would be in vain. (186)
Among the Kṣatriyas who are disciplined in conduct, though they may be emaciated and of meager means, when seekers approach them, what is given to them yields great fruit. (187)
A righteous person should not give a gift when asked out of fear, nor to one who has done him a favor, nor to those whose character is dancing and singing, nor to jesters. 188.
If your mother or father are petitioners for your life, you must give it to them; for they indeed acquired it for you. (189)
The suffering that parents endure in carrying a child in the womb cannot be repaid, even in hundreds of years. (190)
Associate with the poor, O son of Kuntī, and do not bestow wealth upon the wealthy;
medicine is beneficial for the diseased, but what use is medicine to one who is healthy? (191)
One who does not beg and is in distress must be restrained by all possible means;
yet, compassion is the supreme dharma when that which is requested is given. 192.
One should not despise a petitioner nor should one ever turn them away; even when given to an outcaste or a dog, a gift is never lost. (193)
Who would despise one who begs day after day, like a teacher, and who performs daily purification, just as one polishes a mirror? (194)
Indeed, there is nothing more sinful in all the worlds than this: neither self-destruction nor the begging of "give me, give me" (dehi). ||195||
Wretched men, though they train themselves, do not restrain themselves when asked, "Give!
Such is the state of one who does not give; may you never become like this! (196)
One should give simply because it ought to be given, and one should sacrifice simply because it ought to be sacrificed;
let there be the fruit of heaven or let there not be, for indeed, action must be performed by a person.
The gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of land—these indeed are purifying gifts that deliver one in the hereafter. (198)
Gold, silver, garments, jewels, pearls, and wealth—all these riches you bestow, O Great King. (199)
He who gives away an auspicious tawny cow (kapilā) together with a garment, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and possessing horns tipped with gold—
she, indeed, becoming a wish-fulfilling cow through those various qualities, [grants his desires].
That cow approaches the man who gives her away. ||200||
The man who gives fragrant incenses, ointments, bathing powders, and garlands to the twice-born shall become free from disease.
Likewise, he is handsome in the world of the gods. ||201||
Give sesame seeds, give water, give lamps; do not boast.
Rejoice with your kinsmen; this is very difficult to obtain after death.
Water, my dear, is difficult to obtain, especially in the next world;
by the gift of water, eternal satisfaction is attained. (203)
The man who gives light becomes possessed of vision and endowed with radiance;
the giver of a lamp shines like a garland of lamps in the heavenly world. (204)
O best of the Bharatas, he who gives a field to a twice-born man dwells in the world of Cakra, being honored by hosts of apsarases. (205)
But he who gives a pair of sandals provided with smooth oil shall also attain the worlds, honored by the deities. (206)
Even if one were to give away all one's possessions with a defiled inner self, one does not attain heaven by that; the mind alone is the cause in this matter.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is beloved in the home, that very thing should be given to one who possesses virtue by one who wishes for that [gift] to be inexhaustible. (208)
That which is given to the twice-born with due honor is the most excellent;
indeed, that which is given when requested is called mediocre by the wise. (209)
Whatever is given with contempt, or even without faith,
that the sages who speak the truth call the lowest form of gift.
Whatever is offered, given, or performed as austerity without faith, O Pārtha, is said to be "unreal"; it yields no fruit either in this world or after death.
For even to one who asks for mere nose-cleansing rags or leafy vegetables, one should give;
indeed, because of such practice, one will eventually give even meat and other such things. (212)
He who, having made a promise, does not give—whether it be little or much—has all his hopes destroyed, like the lost actions of a eunuch. (213)
For one who has promised "I shall do it" but fails to perform that duty,
his merit from sacrifices and charitable works is destroyed, as he is consumed by his false speech.
The ritual of the single fire, the oblation offered in the *troṭā*, and whatever gift is given within the sacrificial altar (*antarvedi*)—that is designated as *iṣṭa*. (215)
Reservoirs, wells, tanks, temples, the gift of food, and groves—these are designated as *pūrta* (meritorious works of public utility). ||216||
Generally, a man dreads death;
yet some await death as they would a welcome guest. 217.
How can those who have abandoned the mud of their homes sleep happily during the nights, when their births in the hells are separated from death only by an interval? (218)
Whoever gives unblemished food to one who is traveling on a road and is exhausted, having not seen a village for a long time, gains great merit as the fruit of that deed. (219)
O dear one,
he who dispels the hunger of one who is emaciated, modest, exhausted, and sinking down— there is no one equal to him in merit.
The great fruit belongs to both the recipient and the giver; this is directly perceived by those who rejoice.
Other gifts, moreover, have their results beyond the range of sight.
To one who is weary, shelter should be given; likewise, a seat to one who is fatigued; water to one who is thirsty, and food to one who is hungry. ||222||
One should give sight, or one should give the mind, or one should give speech that is well-spoken; one should rise to greet others and approach them with proper conduct and courtesy. (223)
Grass for a seat, ground for resting, water, and kind speech—these are never withheld from the virtuous in the homes of the good. (224)
Know those gods who do not eat first, nor honor the elderly, guests, and children, to be nothing but Rākṣasas, devoid of hospitality and auspiciousness. 225.
One should not eat delicious food alone; one should not contemplate one's own welfare alone; one should not travel the road alone; nor should one remain awake alone among those who are asleep. 226.
For those whose teacher does not cook, whose mother does not cook, and whose father does not cook,
and who desire leftovers— for them, this is great happiness.

His strength is for the sake of the weak, and his acquisition is for the sake of renunciation; his ripening is for the sake of those whose merit has diminished—by him, therefore, the ancestors truly possess a son. (228)
O dear one, kinsmen and relatives live in dependence upon him,
just as all beings depend on the rain-cloud and birds depend on a tree that bears sweet fruit.
When a kinsman, having approached a wealthy relative, nevertheless suffers, he censures that relative's home as a deer does a burnt tree. (230)
O dear one, let these four dwell in the house of one endowed with prosperity according to the duties of a householder:
a destitute kinsman, one who has fallen on hard times, and a man of noble birth.
The friend is poor, and the sister is childless. ||231||
One who is habitually inactive, gluttonous, hated by the world, highly deceitful, cruel,
ignorant of place and time, and of disagreeable appearance—
One should not allow these to dwell in one's house. ||232||
Sacrificial priests, family chaplains, and teachers; disciples, kinsmen, and relatives—all who are endowed with learning and virtuous conduct are to be honored and revered. (233)
Those who harbor malice toward their preceptor, father, or mother, whether by thought or by deed,
their sin is no different from that of killing an embryo.
There is no other evildoer in the world besides him. ||234||
O Bhārata, the father and the mother create this body;
but that birth which the teacher ordains is divine, free from old age, and immortal. (235)
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge—whichever a man has studied, he should first offer his salutation to that [teacher]. 236.
A wise person should never harbor persistent enmity toward their teacher; rather, when the teacher is angry, he should be honored and propitiated. 237.
In this world, one must behave properly toward a teacher even when he acts wrongly;
there is no doubt that reviling a teacher destroys the lifespan of human beings. (238)
One who possesses austerity and purity, and who constantly delights in dharma and truth, should properly perform the worship of mother and father every single day. (239)
A mother is weightier than the earth; a father is higher than the sky.
The mind is swifter than the wind; anxiety is greater than a blade of grass. 240.
O Indra among kings, when both father and mother are satisfied by an embodied being,
his fame shall be eternal both in this world and after death.

The giver of life (the father), the one who provides food (the grandfather), and the one who eats the food (the great-grandfather)—these three are said to be the ancestors (pitṛs) in the performance of the ancestral rites. ||242||
The son brings joy to the father, and the father indeed is the son;
the gifts that ought to be given, the father alone bestows. ||243||
Whether he is capable or incapable, emaciated or robust, the mother alone protects her son; there is no other nourisher like her. (244)
He grieves, yet he does not exert his own effort;
for even though he is bereft of fortune, he maintains the conviction, "This is my home. (245)
He who has taken refuge with his mother— even though he has sons and grandsons—
remains there in the sky at the end of even a hundred years.
Then Bhī is prosperous, then Bhī is tranquil;
then the world is empty when it is not separated from me. ||247||
He should salute him, offer him a seat, and attend upon him with joined palms;
when he departs, he should follow behind him. 248.
The vital breaths of a young man rise upward when old age approaches; he recovers them again by rising to greet others and by saluting them. (249)
For one who is habitually respectful and serves the elders, four things increase: reputation, lifespan, fame, and strength. (250)
Furthermore, his age, lineage, and noble birth, as well as the conformity of his dress, speech, and intellect, and his sanity [are to be examined]. (251)
A person should offer consolation to one who is despondent, dejected, agitated, afflicted by hunger, tormented by disease, robbed of wealth, or distressed by calamity. (252)
One should always practice the conduct prescribed by the wise and properly established for one's own community, remaining free from sloth. (253)
A living being who has fallen away from right conduct does not attain happiness;
for one who is endowed with right conduct becomes a partaker of prosperity. 254.
On the new moon day, the fourteenth, and on the eighth and fourteenth days of the lunar fortnights,
a twice-born man who has completed his ritual bath after Vedic study should remain celibate.
One should not desire what is not given according to the vows of restraint and observance; one should not drink intoxicants, nor harm living beings, nor speak falsehood.
He who desires to enter heaven as if it were his own home should not even mentally desire the wife of another. (256)
Abstaining from dancing, singing, instrumental music, perfumes, garlands, vehicles, pride, luxurious beds, and intoxicants, he eats moderately during the sacred festival days.
He attains the imperishable worlds of the Maruts. ||257||

A wise person should constantly practice the restraints (yamas), but not exclusively the observances (niyamas). For by failing to practice the restraints, one falls, whereas by devoting oneself solely to the observances, one does not. ||258||
Compassion, patience, truthfulness, non-violence, self-restraint, straightforwardness, affection, serenity, sweetness, and gentleness are the ten *yamas*. (259)
Charity, sacrifice, austerity, meditation, study of the scriptures, restraint of the generative organ, vows, fasting, silence, and purification—these are the ten observances (niyamas). 260.
Wealth should be acquired through righteousness; wealth obtained through righteousness is of three kinds. A man should strive diligently to make righteousness his supreme goal. (261)
One who desires land should accomplish the purpose of dharma with one part, the purpose of pleasure with one part, and he should cause the remaining one part to increase. ||262||
Those objects which are obtained through righteousness are to be attained; as for those obtained by unrighteous means, fie upon them!
One should never abandon the eternal dharma in this world out of a desire for wealth.
For one who desires wealth for the sake of Dharma, the absence of desire is superior;
for it is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off. 264.
Among all forms of purity, purity regarding wealth is preeminent;
for he who is pure in regard to wealth is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water. (265)
Do not set your mind upon those objects which are acquired through great hardship, by transgressing the Dharma, or by bowing down before an enemy. (266)
For greed destroys the wisdom of one born into a noble family who covets the wealth of others; and wisdom, when destroyed, destroys prosperity. (267)
Dharma, artha, and kāma—these three are the fruits of life;
these three should be attained while remaining entirely free from unrighteousness (adharma). 268.
One should make each day fruitful through dharma, pleasure, and wealth;
for when that day has passed, one's life is diminished by that much. (269)
That birth of living beings which is for neither Dharma, nor wealth, nor pleasure, nor peace, is in vain; it leads solely to death. (270)
Renounce wealth for the sake of worthy recipients, cultivate the virtues born of desire, and do what is pleasing to those you hold dear; for victorious Death hastens.

For one there is happiness here but not in the next world; for another, it is in the next world but not here. For one there is happiness both here and in the next world; for another, it is neither in the next world nor here. ||272||
For those who possess abundant wealth and always delight, well-adorned,
this world— the slayer of the foremost of enemies— is theirs.
He is not [so] for those who are always attached to bodily pleasure. ||273||
Those who are disciplined in yoga, devoted to austerity, habituated to sacred study, who wear away their bodies,
have conquered their senses, and are intent on the welfare of all beings— [they go there].
For them, this world is not [the place] where that slayer of enemies resides. ||274||
Those who first practice the Dharma itself, and having acquired wealth through righteousness at the proper time,
obtain wives and perform sacrifices with that wealth.
For them, there is neither this world nor the next. ||275||
Those unfortunate ones who possess neither knowledge, nor austerity, nor charity, nor even perform worship or sacrifice with rituals,
do not attain happiness.
For them, both this world and the next exist. ||276||
O Indra among kings, he who undertakes pilgrimages, is free from anger, is of truthful character, firm in his vows,
and treats all beings as himself— such a person enjoys the fruit of the sacred fords. (277)
Without fasting for three nights, without visiting sacred fords,
and without giving gold and cows, one is born indeed as a poor man.
For even those who are always poor, O lord of men, are able to attain the merit of visiting sacred fords, which is superior even to sacrifices. (279)
A poor man is as one dead; a kingdom without a protector is dead;
a funeral rite performed by one ignorant of the Vedas is dead; and a sacrifice without sacrificial fees is dead. (280)
From famine to famine, from terror to even greater terror, and from death to further death go the poor who commit evil deeds. (281)
No one accepts beneficial words spoken even at the right time by a poor man who is both unwise and destitute. (282)
Even if they exist, the other virtues do not shine when their primary purpose has been lost;
for prosperity is the illuminator of virtues among living beings, just as the sun is for all creatures. (283)
The outcaste and the pauper—these two are considered equal:
for the outcaste, people do not take [from him], and for the pauper, they do not give [to him]. (284)
A house devoid of gold, lacking servants, and possessing little food, grain, or cattle is the supreme treasure of hell for those who are miserly and afflicted by distress.
O King, he who is lean in his wealth, lean in his servants, and lean in his guests—he indeed is "lean" (kṛśa) by name; one who is merely lean in body is not truly lean.
For one who enjoys the wealth of friends by fulfilling their desired requests, yet is unable to repay them, death is better than life. (287)
O King, a person who is poor by nature does not suffer as much as one who, having enjoyed prosperity and grown accustomed to happiness, is later deprived of those very blessings. (288)
Generally, O King of kings, those who possess wealth lack the digestive power to eat; however, for the poor, even food with vegetables is digested.
The poor always eat food that is far more excellent; hunger produces a sense of deliciousness that is not found among the wealthy. (290)
Hunger dispels the notion of dharma and takes away one's fortitude;
the tongue, following after objects of sense, drags one toward flavors. (291)
Having encountered adverse circumstances, the ignorant man blames the gods;
the unwise man does not recognize the faults of his own actions. (292)
If, despite striving and undertaking efforts, one does not acquire wealth, one should practice great austerity; for what is not sown does not grow.
When fate is utterly adverse and human effort is rendered futile, for a spirited man who is poor, where else but the forest can there be happiness? (294)
For one who has been rejected despite his wealth, and whose mind is tormented by adversity, what cause for hatred is there in a penance grove when the suffering is the same? (295)

Blessings upon the birth of even a tree that is humpbacked, worm-eaten, scorched by forest fires, with its bark white with age, and standing in barren soil; but not so for one who is a petitioner. (296)
"Come here! Go away! Sit down! Stand up! Speak! Observe silence!"—thus do the wealthy play with supplicants who are seized by the crocodile of hope. (297)
Day after day, Prajāpati indeed creates living beings;
yet even today he does not create a single one who does not despise a suppliant. (298)
Hoarseness in the throat, perspiration on the face, discoloration, and trembling—
those very same signs that belong to one who is dying also belong to one who is begging.
Just as contact perfumes clothing, water, sesame seeds,
and the earth with the fragrance of flowers through their proximity, so too do qualities arise from association. (300)
For intelligence, O dear one, declines through association with the inferior;
it attains equality with equals and excellence through association with the superior. (301)
Even a small quality attains expansion among those possessed of virtues, like a drop of oil fallen upon a mass of sweet-smelling water. (302)
Even that which is great becomes small when it is in one devoid of qualities; the expansion of qualities [shrinks] according to the nature of its support, like a lordly elephant in a mirror. (303)
Therefore, one should delight in virtues and never in faults;
for he who is devoid of virtue is called a fool by himself.

A virtuous person should sit only with the virtuous and form associations with the virtuous; he should cultivate friendship with the virtuous and should not engage in anything whatsoever with the wicked. (305)
He does not rejoice in honor, nor is he distressed when reviled;
he does not speak harsh words when provoked to anger—they call him one who possesses the marks of a virtuous man.
They do not remember offenses, but rather they remember good deeds; these virtuous ones, the best of men, do not violate the noble boundaries of conduct. 307.
Just as the abundance of crops in excellent fields increases, so too does the virtuous person bow down under the weight of his branches and fruit. (308)
They do not speak ill behind one's back, they uplift those who are distressed, and they do not despise those living with them; O Indra among kings, such virtuous people are worthy of service.
He who, having attained great wealth as well as knowledge and the status of a teacher, conducts himself without arrogance, is called a wise man. (310)
If it is not possible to follow the entire path of the virtuous, one should follow it even slightly; for one who remains on the path does not perish.
Not only does such a person become virtuous and esteemed by these people, but even his own self holds him in high regard as one endowed with excellent character. (312)
Having recognized that this noble conduct is an eternal way of life, the virtuous, while acting for the sake of others, do not look for any recompense. (313)

Conduct, which is said to be the highest, must be guarded with effort; for it is conduct that determines one's status. One who is diminished in wealth is not truly diminished, but one who is ruined in conduct is utterly destroyed.
Day after day, one should indeed examine one's own conduct:
"Is this of mine equal to that of beasts, or is it equal to that of virtuous men? (315)
The doer, the one who causes it to be done, and he who approves of it—whether it be good or evil—the fruit for them is equal. (316)
One should not meet evil with evil; one should always remain virtuous.
The wicked person who desires to commit sin is destroyed by his own self. (317)
Just as a stone is raised upon a mountain with great effort, yet falls back down with ease, so too does the self [ascend or descend] through merit and demerit. (318)
The sound of meritorious action touches both heaven and earth;
as long as that sound persists, so long is the person said to exist. (319)
For in this world, fame revives men like a mother, while infamy destroys the life of embodied beings even while they still live. (320)
One must never cause harm to friends, nor to those who trust one; likewise, one should not harm him whose food one has eaten or where one has found shelter. (321)
For the unrighteous, the slayer of a Brahmin, the drunkard, the thief, and the breaker of vows,
atonement has been prescribed by the virtuous; but for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
The path leading to the hells must be traversed by that cruel-hearted person who, though himself sinless, commits evil acts.
The self is certainly dear to that man who commits evil;
yet the self does not experience the evil committed by the self alone. (324)
One whose karma is defiled, who is exceedingly negligent, constantly untruthful, and lacking firm devotion;
one whose passion is drawn out and who possesses great pride.
One should not associate with these six lowest of men. ||325||
Because of association with evildoers, even those who are sinless suffer; the same fault touches them due to their mixed state.
By being mixed, the moist is burned by the dry.
Therefore, one should not form an alliance with the wicked. ||326||
A wicked person should be avoided by one of great intelligence, for he brings about harm both through alliance and enmity, whether by licking or by biting. (327)
There are only two ways to deal with thorns and wicked people: either by wearing shoes or by breaking their faces, or else by avoiding them from afar. (328)
Do not place your trust in the wicked, thinking "he is my long-time acquaintance";
for a serpent, even if approached over a long period of time, will surely bite.
A base person mounts one who is virtuous and humble with discipline, just as a lowly creature climbs upon a wild elephant that has sat down after creating a staircase from its own body.
O virtuous ones, do not place your trust in a wicked person simply because he bows;
for who is there that does not stoop like a scale, yet remains a thief of the water from the well? (331)
A virtuous person should be content with the wicked even when they do not inflict harm;
it is no loss at all if one who is coiled by a serpent is not bitten.
Even sweet words spoken by a wicked person produce terror in me, like flowers out of season. (333)
Truth must be sought within the sweet, yet it is not there, and from that [sweetness] comes immortality;
dharma must be sought within the harsh, yet it is not there, and from that [harshness] comes poison.
Even if one cuts a neem tree with an axe, anoints it with honey and ghee,
and worships it with perfumes and garlands, it remains bitter in every respect.
A treatise that pacifies the pride of the wise produces pride in the wicked;
just as light that clarifies the vision of others causes blindness in owls.

Pride of learning, pride of wealth, and thirdly, pride of supernatural powers—these indeed are the intoxications of the arrogant; yet these very same things serve as the means of self-restraint for the virtuous. (337)
It bends, it joins together, it melts, and it is heated;
can iron ever be compared to the mind of a wicked person? (338)
Oh, how great is the skill of the wicked in concealing their misdeeds, such that they are not perceived even as they burn, like a fire of chaff that lacks visible flames! 339.
Alas! What great misery! This world is indeed perverse, in that the virtuous man feels shame while the wicked man rejoices.
A wicked person sees the faults of others even when they are as small as a mustard seed, yet though seeing his own faults as large as a bilva fruit, he does not see them.
Just as the virtuous attain peace by honoring those who are elder, so does the fool find satisfaction by reviling the good. (342)
One who is wealthy yet does not give, one who is poor yet high-minded, and one who is unlearned yet arrogant— they say these are the characteristics of those with joyful minds.
A man who, while himself behaving in such a manner, casts blame upon another for his fault, and who becomes angry despite being powerless, is a most foolish person. (344)
A wicked person indeed considers gentle speech to be born of incapacity; one should recognize that the objective has been won when there is softness toward a stone. (345)
When the wicked are occasionally requested by the virtuous to perform some task, it is well known that they consider themselves to be virtuous while [the requesters] are wicked. 346.
Even a wise man, having heard the auspicious and inauspicious words of men who are prattling,
adopts the speech of the virtuous, just as a swan takes milk from water.
Though urged toward evil, the virtuous soul does not consent to it;
though restrained from evils, the wicked soul desires evil. (348)
The suffering of one who lacks character when it is heard; the wealth of one who lives as a miser; the enthusiasm of one who is unfortunate; and the strength of a coward. (349)

Just as water in a skull, or milk in a dog-skin bag, [becomes impure] through the defect of its container, so too does sacred learning [become defiled] when residing in one devoid of right conduct. (350)
Knowledge acquired through unjust means does not cover one's private parts, nor does it ward off gadflies and mosquitoes; like the tail of a dog, it serves no purpose. (351)
What inheritance does the world have from past karma? What kinship does it possess?
What things urge us on here? We are under the power of what? (352)
Just as a calf finds its mother among thousands of cows, so does the fruit of good and evil deeds follow the doer. (353)
Just as flowers and fruits, even when not being urged on,
do not overstep their own proper time, so too did those [ancient ones] act in the past.
Whatever good or evil one performs as a child, a youth, or an old man, one experiences the results in those very same stages of life, birth after birth. (355)
Those who are devoid of splendor, lacking great energy, unwise, and deprived of their hands and feet, have fallen into a state of servitude. (356)
And there is a great disparity among those who have bound themselves to duty:
some carry the palanquin, while others walk having already reached the palanquin. (357)
He desires to become higher and higher in the world; he exerts himself with great effort, yet he does not proceed accordingly. ||358||
Honor and dishonor, gain and loss, decline and prosperity—these proceed or turn back by the power of destiny at every step. (359)
He who steals, impoverishes, strikes down, kills,
or fails to honor those worthy of honor—
whatever merit a man sows, he reaps that very same thing.
He enjoys the fruits resulting from that [action]. ||360||
That one thing is sown and another is produced is not tenable;
whatever seed is sown in the earth, that very same thing sprouts forth.
Happiness is certain in heaven; happiness is found in both [heaven and earth] here on earth; in hell there is only suffering; but in liberation, however, there is absolute happiness. (362)
O King, these five auspicious things— wells, gardens, assembly halls, water-stations, and dwellings— lead this person to the heavenly world.
One should do today what must be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what belongs to the afternoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one has finished this or that. (364)
Death is that which would be death; he who would be immortal is indeed a friend to death.
It is fitting for you to tell me this: "This shall happen tomorrow. (365)
What portion of infinite time is a hundred autumns? How can one whose life is so brief afford to sleep? (366)
Even that which is already extremely brief is further diminished by night, which steals away its vitality;
half of even that is further reduced by disease, grief, old age, and death. (367)
This entire world is sinking into the deep ocean of time, which has old age and death for its great crocodiles; no one perceives this. (368)
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor oblations, nor repeated recitations can protect a human being from death or even from old age. (369)
But he who, having seen one who is old, diseased, or even dead, remains unperturbed and stays as he was before, such a person is truly healthy. (370)
Even after conquering this earth bounded by the oceans, would a man ever fail to encounter old age and death? (371)
Day and night, old age wanders through the world;
death devours beings just as a serpent swallows the wind. (372)
An old woman is unable either to enjoy or to renounce sense objects;
like a toothless dog, she merely licks her own bones with her tongue. (373)
Day by day, death draws closer, like a condemned man being led step by step to the place of execution. (374)
"I shall do this; from that, this will come to pass"—Death does not wait for such a resolve (*saṅkalpa*) as this. (375)
For one who is ripe, there is no fear other than falling;
for a man who is born, there is no fear other than death. ||376||
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of grass. (377)
When death, old age, disease, and many kinds of suffering are constantly attached to the Lord, how can he remain as if healthy? (378)
When death indeed follows those who stand and those who lie down, why do you sleep so happily, my son, like a fish in a small pond? (379)
How will you travel alone along this path through the wilderness of darkness—a road without rest, without provisions, without support, and without a guide? (380)
When one who knows the uneven [pulse] observes a person with fixed, rolling eyes, seized by hiccups, gasping with an extended chest,
as if entering a great darkness or a deep abyss;
Then, where are you, and where are your kinsmen? ||381||
Before old age makes your body decrepit, O you who take away strength,
vigor, and beauty, establish this treasure of merit.
Accumulations of gold and jewels, gathered through both auspicious and inauspicious deeds, do not assist one at the time of the body's dissolution. (383)
Youth is fleeting, wealth is won and lost, health is fragile, and the company of loved ones is transient; he who does not feel attachment to these is a wise man. 384.
One should not place trust in the smallness of fire, disease, or poison, nor likewise in the greatness of health, wealth, or life. (385)
What wise man would place his trust in women, kings, serpents, Vedic study, one who serves an enemy, sensual enjoyments, or the span of life? (386)
Having observed that beings are joined with birth and accompanied by death, as well as by the transformations of old age, and are tormented by diseases.
The wise praise liberation, which is to be realized through one's own direct experience.
The realization of the path of the fathers and the path of the gods is the one enemy; there is no second enemy.
O King, ignorance is equal to [death] for a man;
enveloped by it, he engages in most dreadful sinful deeds. (399)
For this suffering that is experienced arises from ignorance;
that ignorance comes from greed alone, and ignorance is indeed greed itself. (400)
Therefore, one should thoroughly examine the defects arising from ignorance;
and one should constantly abandon the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which originates from ignorance. ||401||
The wise, through the emanations of their wisdom, ferry across the ignorant by means of its fruits;
but the ignorant never ferry others across, nor themselves at any time. (402)
For just as one who is blind suffers hardships on a journey, so does one devoid of knowledge in your world; therefore, the knower of wisdom is superior. (403)
Furthermore, due to union with the undesired and separation from the beloved, men are joined with mental sufferings that are small in measure. (404)
Just as a goldsmith indeed purifies silver in the fire many times with little effort, and not for long even with great exertion.
In the same way, for one born through hundreds of births, purification occurs through a small amount of merit;
however, even with great effort, purification occurs within a single birth. (406)
Just as one might wipe away a small amount of dust from the body with little effort,
yet the removal of a great deal of it requires immense exertion, so too is the removal of faults.
One should eradicate anger through forgiveness; desire by abandoning conceptualization; greed and delusion through contentment; and pride by imparting the truth. 408.
A wise person should avoid hope for the future by abandoning wealth, and should avoid affection through the practice of yoga. 409.
One should conquer delusion and craving through contentment; one should conquer sloth through exertion, and conquer discursive thought through certainty. 410.
Having abandoned pride, one becomes dear; having abandoned desire, one becomes happy.
Having abandoned anger, one is free from affliction; having conquered craving, one does not suffer. ||411||
O dear one, those who seek liberation must certainly conduct themselves within their own proper domain;
however, the wise man should completely avoid that which is characterized by passion for desire. 412.
In this world, the discipline of not desiring, not touching, and not even looking [at objects of sense] should be practiced by a person for the sake of abandoning passion. (413)
Passion is born from conceptual construction; when indulged in, it increases.
It departs through non-indulgence and through the knowledge of reality for the wise.
S9. May your mind be content with whatever wealth you have, like the foot of one wearing sandals upon a ground covered with deerskin. 415.
As it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika-vyākhyā*: "Thinking that cattle, women, and even one's own body are not sufficient as wealth, one should attain tranquility. (416)
One should not dwell on those things that have passed away as being non-existent;
for if one disregards them, affection perishes.
For an embodied being, grief arises from attachment due to the fear of separation;
when one realizes that [attachment] is useless, it perishes immediately. (418)
Sleep should indeed be abandoned, having considered the defects of dreaming;
for in sleep, the embodied being is overwhelmed by passion (rajas) or darkness (tamas). 419.
One who seeks the highest good should avoid wandering at night, sleeping during the day, laziness, sexual intercourse, intoxication, dejection, and the company of the wicked. (420)
Due to the wickedness of his speech, his fickleness, and the instability of his mind, he remains in states of misery. (421)
He never finds the resolve to turn back from his course,
like a kapiñjala bird pursuing the shadow of a hawk in the heat of the sun.
Desire is never quenched by the enjoyment of desired objects;
rather, it increases all the more, like a fire fed with clarified butter. 423.
There is nothing else on earth more sinful than women;
even when merely contemplated in the mind, women are the root of all calamities. (424)
Villages and market towns are ruined by women; buying and selling are ruined by women.
Women are the root of all misfortunes; therefore, one should not embrace them.
The Ender, the wind, death, the netherworld, the submarine fire, the razor’s edge, poison, the serpent, and fire—on one side are these; on the other side is woman. (426)
Just as a net is for fish, a cage for a bird, or a snare with all its loops for a fool, so is the fair-eyed woman a bond. (427)
There is no one inaccessible to them, nor do they have any regard for age;
whether he is ugly or handsome, they enjoy him simply because he is a man.
Out of fear of men and likewise out of dread of dishonor, women— who are otherwise beyond restraint— remain within the bounds of propriety toward their husbands, even when they are not solicited.
Whatever treatise Uśanas knows and whatever Bṛhaspati knows—these two do not excel; rather, the intellect of women excels them both. (430)
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor is a beautiful-eyed woman with men. 431.
Even if one were to possess a thousand tongues and live for a hundred autumns,
if one were single-mindedly devoted to this task, one would not meet death by speaking of the faults of women.
A woman is like glowing coals, and a man is like a jar of clarified butter;
those who are attached to her are melted away, while those who remain steadfast are established in their true state.
That which is called "woman" is indeed illusion, deceit, anger, envy, and strife;
a wise man should cast far away that ignoble thing as if it were blazing filth.
The very nature of women is the corruption of men in this world;
thus indeed do the wise never become heedless toward women.
In whichever parts of the body are utterly loathsome, to those very parts people remain attached; by what means, then, will they attain detachment? (436)
For what wise person among men, even knowing [the truth], would not be brought low by a mere deer-skin, as small as a doe's footprint? (437)
With its gaping wound, smeared with the filth of perspiration and discharging urine and blood, the entire world was rendered blind. (438)
His banks are not cast down, nor is he excavated in any way;
rather, it is the digger who goes to ruin through both strength and wealth. (439)
Those very foul-smelling apertures of women that carry away impurities are indeed the objects of desire; oh, what a mockery for men! 440.
One should not listen to talk about women, nor should one look at them when they are naked;
for from seeing them occasionally, the menstrual flow may enter even the weak.
One should not sit in a secluded place with one's mother, sister, or daughter;
for the powerful collection of the senses drags away even a learned man.
Just as the fire within the hollow of a tree might burn that tree entirely down to its roots,
so too should one destroy passion and hatred for the sake of Dharma in this world. (443)
Desire alone is the one bond; there is no other bond here.
For one who is liberated from the bond of desire is fit for becoming Brahman. 444.
He who restrains his anger, who endures harsh speech, and who,
though tormented, does not torment others— he is truly a vessel for profound peace.
What anger can there be for that which is spoken falsely, since it is not so?
And what anger can there be even for that which is spoken truly, since it remains so even when unspoken? (446)
A person overcome by passion is led astray by desire;
first, longing arises, and from that, craving proceeds. ||447||
Craving—craving indeed is the most wicked of all things; it constantly causes agitation for human beings, abounds in unrighteousness, is terrible, and is followed by evil consequences. (448)
Repeatedly showing me the enjoyments that were close at hand,
my thirst has led me far away, like a goat lured by a handful of green grass.
Youth is seized by old age; health is taken away by diseases;
life is overtaken by death; only craving remains unassailed. 450.
The hair of an aging person decays; the teeth of an aging person decay.
But the hope for wealth and the hope for life do not decay, even in one who is aging.
There is no substance in the world that could satisfy craving;
a person who is like the ocean can never be filled. (452)
Just as the horn of a cow grows as it grows in time, even so does craving grow as wealth increases. (453)
Like an unchaste woman, craving impels a person toward what ought not to be done;
but shame, like a mother, protects that very same person from all evils. (454)
Craving is the enemy that causes turmoil for these three worlds;
for those by whom it has been cast off like a snake's slough, who is poor and who is a lord? (455)

That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays, and which is a disease that ends only with life—that craving, for one who abandons it, there is happiness. (456)
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the exhaustion of craving. (457)
Greed alone is the great predator; from greed, evil proceeds.
From that evil comes the acquisition of unrighteousness, and from that, suffering proceeds. ||458||
Know, O best of men, that greed alone is the foundation of all evils;
even highly learned men, when possessed by greed, commit sinful deeds. (459)
Discontent leads only to unhappiness, and from greed comes the delusion of the senses; consequently, his wisdom perishes, just as knowledge is lost when devoid of practice. (460)
There is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired;
there is suffering in its loss and suffering in its depletion—fie on wealth, which only increases suffering! (461)
They cause delusion in times of prosperity and torment in times of adversity; they weary one at the time of acquisition—when, then, will enjoyments bring happiness? (462)

For those possessed of wealth, there is constant fear from kings, from water, from fire, from thieves, and even from their own kinsmen, just as for living beings there is constant fear of death. (463)
For just as meat in the sky is devoured by birds, on the ground by beasts of prey, and in the water by fish, so too is a man of wealth consumed by everyone. 464.
Since accumulation ends in destruction, life ends in death, and union ends in separation, who would set their heart upon wealth? (465)
Renouncing their dear lives, some men enter the field of battle;
others, seeking wealth, depart for the state of servitude.
Who would desire this body, which is the locus of defects, destined for ruin, and subject to decay—since it inevitably produces agitation both in prosperity and in adversity? (467)
O Great King, three intoxications delude the undiscerning: women, food, and drink; those who are attached to these do not remain awake. 468.
Prosperity and women are as transient as the crests of waves; what wise man would take delight in them, which are like the shade cast by the hoods of a serpent? (469)
Do not, my dear father, become overly prolix, deluded by worldly prosperities;
for even the heavens become a burden when the turn of destiny changes.
Between the state of possessing nothing and sovereignty, there is this very great distinction:
for the wealthy man is perpetually anxious, whereas by renouncing everything, one becomes happy. (471)
For no one who harbors doubt is seen to be free from affliction; therefore, one who knows the highest truth abandons both accumulations and suffering simultaneously.
When the drum of opposition is beaten by ordinary city-dwellers against the king, that very sentiment of "Do not do so! is what causes him pleasure. (473)
He who perceives that wealth is difficult to obtain in this world, while afflictions and suffering for the sake of family are easily encountered, is liberated.
Enough with possession itself; one who possesses things is full of faults.
For the silkworm is indeed bound by its own cocoon. (475)
As many dear attachments as a living being forms with the mind, so many spikes of sorrow are driven into his heart. (476)
Mental attachment is said to be the root of suffering;
through attachment, a living being becomes entangled and undergoes the conjunction with suffering. (477)
Living beings, attached to their sons, wives, and families, sink down like aged wild elephants submerged in the ocean-like mud of a lake. (478)
This very poison consisting of sons and wife is difficult to conquer in this world, having drunk which, deluded beings are born and die. (479)

Just as one would cast off worms born from one's own body that are not perceived as oneself, so too should one cast off those perceived as sons who are born from oneself but are not truly one's own. 480.
Where there is attachment, there is fear; attachment is a vessel for suffering.
Sufferings have their root in attachment; when that is abandoned, there is great happiness. (481)
One whose mind is set on liberation should not worry about one's own kin, thinking, "O father, how will these people fare without me? (482)
A living being is born by itself and grows by itself;
likewise, it encounters happiness, suffering, and death by itself. (483)
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart, so too is the meeting of living beings. (484)
