In this way, one should not form excessive attachment toward sons, kinsmen, or friends, for separation from them is certain. (485)
Thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives, have passed away in age after age; to whom do they belong, or to whom do we belong? (486)
This permanent cohabitation is never to be found by anyone, even with one's own body, let alone with anyone else. (487)
They have come from the unseen and have gone back to the unseen;
they do not belong to you, nor do you belong to them—what cause for lamentation is there in that? (488)
When wealth is lost, or when a wife, a son, or a father has died, one should reflect, "Alas, what misery! and thus practice the alleviation of grief.
He who grieves for what is dead or lost, or for what is past, gains sorrow through sorrow and encounters two misfortunes. (490)
This is the medicine for suffering: that one should not dwell upon it;
for when it is dwelled upon, it does not depart, but rather increases further still. (491)
O King, either wealth abandons a man, or a man abandons his wealth; this is inevitable, and one who knows this should have no doubt. (492)
Even before this, this understanding should be formed by you who possess discernment:
that all this is impermanent, including both "I" and "mine. (493)
One who has fixed their mind on impermanence grieves over a withered garland; one who has fixed their mind on permanence grieves over a broken vessel. (494)
Fire arises by itself;
he who, being burned by that fire, experiences intense heat, is not a wise man. //495//
Pleasure and pain, existence and non-existence, gain and loss, death and life—
all these touch everyone here in turn.
Therefore, the wise person should neither grieve nor rejoice.
Enjoy happiness when it arrives; endure suffering when it arrives.
One should wait for what has come through time, just as a farmer waits for his crops.
Whether it be happiness or suffering that has befallen living beings, all must be experienced by those who are powerless; there is no way to avoid it. (498)
Suffering follows immediately after happiness, and happiness follows immediately after suffering;
they revolve around a person in alternation, like the spokes of a wheel's rim. (499)
Only the man possessed of knowledge, joined with supreme wisdom, knowing indeed the rising and setting [of all things], neither grieves nor exults.
One should destroy mental suffering with wisdom and physical suffering with medicines;
for this is the power of knowledge, which the foolish do not attain. 501.
For by mental suffering the body is tormented, just as water contained in a jar is heated by a red-hot iron ball. (502)
Therefore, one should pacify the mind with wisdom, as one quenches fire with water;
for when his mind is stilled, his physical suffering comes to rest.
The wrinkles do not agree with one another, nor do the gray hairs recognize each other;
for those who have realized the truth through wisdom, there is no further rebirth here.
One whose mind is undisturbed by sorrows, who is free from longing amidst pleasures, and who is devoid of passion, fear, and anger—he is called a sage of steady wisdom. (505)
Thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for fear assail the fool day after day, but not the wise man.
For by attaining wisdom, a person indeed crosses over all evil; freed from taint, he attains purity, and established in purity, he becomes serene. (507)
Even while dwelling in the midst of sense-objects, the wise man does not truly dwell there; whereas the fool, though not dwelling in sense-objects, dwells in them as if he were.
Just as gold mixed with iron does not shine when it has been smelted, so too the wisdom of one whose defilements are undigested does not manifest. //509//
Just as seeds scorched by fire do not sprout again, so too the self is not bound again by hair [of afflictions] consumed by knowledge. 510
Just as the track of birds in the sky or of fish in water cannot be seen,
so too is the course of those who possess knowledge.
Thus ends the *Sārasamuccaya*.
